validity.recommendation: No change to existence/classification. Recommend a follow-up cross-check against sibling PID P7461 'Tyonek Gas Pipeline' to fully close out the naming-overlap question the brief flagged, though current evidence points to non-duplication.
validity.researcher_notes: Existence and non-duplication independently confirmed. The 2014 RCA public notice (Docket P-14-025) names 'Hilcorp Alaska, LLC d/b/a Kenai Nikiski Pipeline (KNPL)' as one of FIVE originally-separate CPCN-holding pipeline entities (Kenai Beluga Pipeline LLC, Beluga Pipeline Company, Kenai Kachemak Pipeline LLC, Hilcorp d/b/a CIGGS, and Hilcorp d/b/a KNPL, holding CPCN Nos. 448/711/668/689) that were consolidated into a single CPCN (668, operated by KBPL) in 2014 -- i.e. KNPL is a genuinely distinct, historically-registered pipeline entity, not a relabeling of any of its Cook Inlet siblings (P7450 Beluga, P7454 Kenai Kachemak, P7455 CIGGS). Checked specifically against the brief's flagged name-collision candidate, P7461 'Tyonek Gas Pipeline' (Nikiski-to-Beluga, 50.7 mi): Alaska DNR DOG's Pipeline Services registry lists a separate 'Tyonek W 10 Gas Pipeline' entry, and PHMSA's 2018 Cook Inlet Pipeline Inventory Report independently describes the Tyonek Platform pipeline system as running from the offshore Tyonek Platform to an LNG plant in Nikiski (and, once the W10 line was completed in late 2018, on to Hilcorp's onshore Beluga pipeline on the west side of Cook Inlet) -- a materially different route and purpose (offshore-platform-to-LNG-plant/Beluga-side gathering) than a 17.5 mi Nikiski-to-Kenai onshore transmission line. This is corroborating, not exhaustive, evidence; a full side-by-side against P7461's own sourcing is left as a recommended follow-up rather than asserted as fully closed.

cross_row_leads.facts: P7461 'Tyonek Gas Pipeline' (Nikiski-to-Beluga, 50.7 mi) was flagged by the brief as a possible name-collision candidate against this row. This 2014 RCA notice (Docket P-14-025) names KNPL as a distinct, separately-CPCN-registered (Nos. 448/711/668/689 family) entity from Beluga Pipeline Company/KKPL/CIGGS; PHMSA's 2018 Cook Inlet Pipeline Inventory Report separately describes a 'Tyonek Platform' pipeline system (offshore-to-LNG-plant-in-Nikiski, later extended via the 'Tyonek West 10 (W10)' line to Hilcorp's onshore Beluga pipeline) as a materially different route/purpose than this row's Nikiski-to-Kenai onshore transmission segment. Recommend a dedicated pass on P7461 using both documents plus Alaska DNR DOG's separate 'Tyonek W 10 Gas Pipeline' registry entry (https://dog.dnr.alaska.gov/Services/Pipeline/Tyonek%20W%2010%20Gas%20Pipeline) to close this out fully.

Alaska DNR DOG's Kenai Kachemak Pipeline page states: built in three phases (2003/2004/2006 including Happy Valley and Kasilof Extensions); 12.75-in mainline (0.330in/0.500in wall), MAOP 1,480 psig; Kasilof Extension 6.625-in, ~4.2 mi (4.1 mi on State lands); currently leased by Kenai Beluga Pipeline LLC; System Length 46.20 mi (37.30 mi on State lands); Status: Active.

Alaska DNR DOG's CIGGS Pipeline page states CIGGS A (16-in dia, 21 mi, tide/submerged lands) and CIGGS LP (10-in dia, 4.7 mi, buried, Middle Ground Shoals-to-Swanson River Oil Pipeline tie-in) were both built in 1972 and originally carried natural gas, but in 2018 were CONVERTED TO OIL transport as part of the CIPL Cross Inlet Pipeline Extension Project (eliminating the need for the Drift River Oil Terminal) -- a major classification/fuel-type change potentially relevant to that row's current Fuel/PipelineType. Listed diameter 10.75in in one table; System Length 26.00 mi (21.00 mi State lands). PHMSA's 2018 Cook Inlet Pipeline Inventory Report independently corroborates CIGGS as a 'natural gas transmission system' with a 21-mile, 10-inch-diameter offshore 'Dual Marine CIGGS' pair, noting as of Oct 2018 'one of the two pipelines will be converted from gas service to hazardous liquid service' -- consistent with, and slightly more precisely dated than, the DOG page's '2018' conversion claim.

PHMSA's 2018 Cook Inlet Pipeline Inventory Report discusses Hilcorp's onshore 'Beluga pipeline' on the west side of Cook Inlet (destination of the new Tyonek W10 line) and the Tyonek Platform pipeline system generally -- relevant background for the Beluga-family rows (P7450/P7458), though the report does not appear to name a segment called 'Beluga Pipeline' or 'Beluga Transmission Pipeline' verbatim in the portions I reviewed.

summary: P7453 'Kenai Beluga Pipeline' / segment 'Kenai Nikiski Pipeline' (17.5 mi, 20in, Nikiski-to-Kenai, Alaska) is a real, distinct, historically-registered pipeline: the 2014 RCA consolidation notice (Docket P-14-025) names 'Hilcorp Alaska, LLC d/b/a Kenai Nikiski Pipeline (KNPL)' by name as one of five originally-separate CPCN-holding entities (CPCN Nos. 448/711/668/689) folded into Kenai Beluga Pipeline LLC's consolidated system in 2014 -- not a duplicate of sibling rows P7450/P7454/P7455/P7458, and (per PHMSA's 2018 Cook Inlet report and Alaska DNR DOG's separate registry entry) apparently distinct from P7461 Tyonek Gas Pipeline too, though that comparison is flagged as a recommended follow-up rather than fully closed. Status/Fuel/PipelineType/Owner are now properly sourced (Fuel and Owner at tier=high with two independent government/press publishers; PipelineType reverified; Operator filled at tier=medium via a corroborated-but-not-explicit two-source inference, with a known stronger source -- a 2020 PHMSA Final Order, CPF No. 5-2019-0026, naming 'Harvest Alaska, LLC's Kenai-Nikiski Pipeline (KNPL)' together -- read via OCR but left unstaged because its public URL could not be re-verified within this session's tool budget). A significant VALIDITY finding: the existing ref for Status/Fuel/Length/Diameter/Location, https://www.npms.phmsa.dot.gov/, is confirmed to be a non-substantive NPMS landing/navigation page that states nothing pipeline-specific -- it does not actually verify any of the five values it was cited for, and should not be relied on. Length, Diameter, Location, Proposal, Construction, Start, Capacity, Pressure, FuelSource, and SegmentCost all remain genuinely UNRESOLVED after an exhaustive search ladder (RCA notices, PHMSA's 2018 Cook Inlet inventory report, Alaska DNR DOG's pipeline registry -- confirmed to have NO entry for this segment under any name, unlike sibling systems -- and Alaska press); rca.alaska.gov itself is blocked by a DataDome anti-bot challenge with no Wayback capture found, and WebSearch was unavailable all session (budget exhausted by the parallel Cook Inlet agent fan-out). All 15 worklist units reported.
